💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sky, the $3.4 billion lending protocol, is facing mounting pressure across its DeFi ecosystem as a withdrawal crisis coincides with a multibillion-dollar contraction in its stablecoin supply.
  • Crypto market insights provided by Unfolded indicated that the combined supply of Sky's two stablecoins, DAI and USDS, has declined 43% to $7.71 billion from a record $13.62 billion on April 5.
  • DAI plus USDS circulating supply across all chains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sky, the $3.4 billion lending protocol, is facing mounting pressure across its DeFi ecosystem as a withdrawal crisis coincides with a multibillion-dollar contraction in its stablecoin supply.

Crypto market insights provided by Unfolded indicated that the combined supply of Sky's two stablecoins, DAI and USDS, has declined 43% to $7.71 billion from a record $13.62 billion on April 5.

DAI plus USDS circulating supply across all chains. Mid-month readings to Oct. 2026 are approximated from Unfolded’s DefiLlama-based image and rounded to $0.25 billion. Apr. 5 ($13.62B) and Nov. 24 ($7.71B) are the source’s printed observations. No November intermediate levels are invented; the Nov. 19 one-day USDS outflow is reported separately in the source. This area chart is not a native stacked-area view.

Industry observers note that source: Unfolded, Sky DAI and USDS supply graphic (Nov. 24, 2026), sourced from DefiLlama · DefiLlama stablecoin circulating supply, all chains.

In a recent development, USDS alone contracted by $2.03 billion on Nov. 19, losing 39% in a single day as a large holder converted the stablecoin into USDC. Its supply has now fallen 65% from its peak.

Selected monthly snapshots digitized from Unfolded’s chart, generally approximate to $0.25 billion; Nov. 24 DAI ($4.54B) and USDS ($3.17B) are rounded DefiLlama readings consistent with the $7.71B combined endpoint. Earlier pre-USDS observations show DAI only. The Apr. 5 record is excluded here because the original source gives its combined total but not exact separate DAI and USDS balances.

Source: Unfolded, Sky DAI and USDS supply graphic (Nov. 24, 2026), sourced from DefiLlama · DefiLlama stablecoin circulating supply, all chains.

The pressure extends to Sky's governance token, which rose 5% over the past 24 hours to $0.04011 but remains down 23% over the past week and 42% over the past month.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, depositors in Sky's stUSDS lending vault are struggling to access their funds. As of Nov. 24, Spark's dashboard demonstrated just 2,121 USDS available for withdrawals against 158.32 million USDS in vault assets.

The liquidity shortage centers on Sky's stUSDS product, which uses stablecoin deposits to finance loans backed by staked SKY.

DeFi analyst Ignas pointed out that the lending product operates separately from the collateral backing DAI and USDS, as well as the strategies generating returns for ordinary sUSDS savings holders.

However, the sharp decline in SKY's price has intensified concerns over loans taken out by some of the ecosystem's largest participants, particularly Sky co-founder Rune Christensen.

Sources indicate that A Nov. 19 investigation by blockchain analytics firm Bitquery found that Christensen's associated positions were backed by 3.58 billion SKY, representing approximately 15% of the token's circulating supply.

Sources indicate that bitquery identified 25 borrowing transactions without a repayment on the current lending engine between May 2025 and Nov. 19, during which the positions accumulated approximately 10.4 million USDS in unpaid interest.

Three of the four identified positions also fell below their required collateralization thresholds, according to Bitquery's analysis, while automatic liquidations were disabled.

It has been revealed that the four vaults owed 74.46 million USDS as of Nov. 24, while Sky Frontier Foundation owed another 40.17 million USDS. Their combined borrowing represents approximately 72% of the stUSDS vault's assets.

The scale of Christensen's SKY exposure complicates his repayment efforts, as selling substantial quantities on the open market could weaken the token's price and the collateral backing other loans.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 23, Christensen mentioned he was exploring a direct sale of some of his SKY holdings to institutional investors. Crypto entrepreneur Du Jun subsequently expressed interest in acquiring his entire position.

Unlike Christensen, Sky Frontier Foundation already holds stablecoin savings that could substantially reduce its borrowing.

On-chain data reviewed by CryptoSlate highlighted that the foundation held approximately 27.9 million USDS in redeemable savings on Nov. 24.

Deploying those funds would allow the foundation to repay roughly 69% of its outstanding debt without selling SKY, releasing liquidity equivalent to nearly 18% of the stUSDS vault's assets.

The repayment could also substantially reduce the foundation's financing expenses.

A Nov. 23 governance forum post highlighted that the foundation was paying nearly 50% in annualized borrowing costs while earning approximately 3.8% on its savings.

At those rates, repaying 27.9 million USDS would reduce the foundation's net annualized financing costs by approximately $12.8 million.

The foundation previously disclosed that it borrowed against its locked SKY holdings to finance operations, leaving it to determine how much of its savings it can commit to repayment.

However, the speed at which depositors previously drained liquidity shows how short-lived any relief could be under the vault's existing withdrawal mechanism.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 23, Christensen's wallet repaid 3 million USDS. Within 24 seconds, ten withdrawals totaling approximately the same amount followed, with the first two alone accounting for roughly 83% of the repayment.

Recent findings suggest that sky Frontier Foundation could cover much of its loan from savings. The prior repayment highlights how fast cash can be withdrawn.

The foundation’s savings could cover about 69% of the loan. The stUSDS vault pays withdrawals as transactions clear against a shared balance.

The repayment shown for the foundation is conditional on its deciding to deploy its savings. The observed withdrawals were paid from the shared pool and do not identify ultimate recipients or guarantee access after a future repayment.

Use the Nov. 24 block 26,487,346 accrued debt and sUSDS maxWithdraw in USDS. Scale the debt bar using their ratio and subtract the redeemable amount for the residual. The Nov. 23 timeline demonstrates single withdrawals in the repayment block and at +12 seconds, then the aggregate of ten withdrawals through +24 seconds. Values are rounded for display.

Recent findings suggest that the repayment shown for the foundation is conditional on its deciding to deploy its savings. The observed withdrawals were paid from the shared pool and do not identify ultimate recipients or guarantee access after a future repayment.

The rapid depletion has prompted calls for a proportional withdrawal queue that would distribute returning liquidity according to depositors' holdings.

A separate governance proposal would deploy $40 million to $50 million from Sky's reserves to acquire SKY directly from borrowers and apply the proceeds toward their outstanding loans.

Neither proposal has received formal approval, while the foundation has yet to commit its savings toward repayment.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (664 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bitcoinmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Bitcoin Lender Ledn Moves US Clients Onshore With Newly introduced Custody Accounts

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that bitcoin lender Ledn is moving beyond loans.
  • Ledn claims that spread makes buying bitcoin through its app about half the cost of a standard purchase on the most popular U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that ledn has lent against bitcoin since 2018 and has serviced more than $11 billion in loans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that bitcoin lender Ledn is moving beyond loans. The firm rolled out Ledn Custody on Tuesday, a latest account that lets eligible U.S. clients hold bitcoin, gold, stablecoins and U.S. dollars, and buy, sell and swap between them in one place, with no trading fees and a 0.5% spread.

Ledn claims that spread makes buying bitcoin through its app about half the cost of a standard purchase on the most popular U.S. bitcoin apps. The launch also moves Ledn’s U.S. clients, previously served from its Cayman Islands entity, to a U.S. company with a U.S. custodian.

Recent findings suggest that ledn has lent against bitcoin since 2018 and has serviced more than $11 billion in loans. Until now, most of its U.S. clients bought their bitcoin elsewhere and moved it to Ledn to borrow against it. The new account brings that first purchase in-house, from buying through to borrowing.

According to recent reports, A standard bitcoin purchase on the most popular U.S. apps costs about 0.9% to 1.25% once trading fees and spread are included, according to Ledn’s own analysis of published fees from October. That puts Ledn in direct competition with the trading apps where many Americans buy their first bitcoin.

It has been revealed that on a $1,000 purchase, that works out to about $5 at Ledn against $9 to $12.50 elsewhere. Clients can deposit dollars and hold them in the account, or use them to buy bitcoin, gold and stablecoins. BitGo describes the gold option as tokenized gold.

According to recent reports, “What our clients want is to hold hard assets, whether that’s bitcoin, gold or stablecoins,” Ledn co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer Mauricio Di Bartolomeo said. “Most people buy them in one place, keep them in another, and when they need cash, they sell. Now they can do all three in one account.”.

He added that clients can borrow against their bitcoin instead of selling, “with gold to follow.”.

In a recent development, assets in a Ledn Custody account are held for the benefit of each client by an independent qualified custodian, segregated from Ledn’s own assets and never lent out for interest. BitGo Bank & Trust, a unit of BitGo (BTGO), provides the custody and trading services behind the account.

The custody setup is a selling point for a lender that came through 2022. Ledn states it has returned every client’s collateral across two full market cycles, including the collapse that bankrupted Celsius, BlockFi and Voyager. The manufacturer has also published monthly loan book and proof of reserves data.

“We’ve spent eight years earning our clients’ trust as a lender,” Ledn co-founder and CEO Adam Reeds remarked. “If you’re going to be a financial services manufacturer, boring is a good thing. We want to be the reliable, stable place where people build their wealth, not a platform with a million features built for trading.”.

It has been revealed that the onshore move lines up with Washington’s message. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated in May that crypto’s problems stem from “the wild, wild west offshore,” adding, “we got to bring it onshore.” The Clarity Act, the market structure bill he urged Congress to pass, stalled in the Senate in September.

In a recent development, ledn is chasing a major market. More than 67 million Americans now own crypto, or about one in four U.S. adults, according to a May survey. Competition for bitcoin borrowers is also heating up, with Cross River Bank launching its first bitcoin-backed loans this week.

In a recent development, ledn has leaned on the capital markets to fund its lending, selling $188 million in bitcoin-backed bonds in February. The custody account now gives the lender a way to win clients before they ever need a loan.

Ledn Custody accounts will roll out to eligible U.S. individual clients over the coming days. The company looks to add lending against gold and open more U.S. states in the coming weeks.

Waymo halts highway operation nationwide after CA DMV pause

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Waymo has pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after the California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the manufacturer to pause highway operation in the state, following a viral video showing a Waymo trying to pass a police blockade.
  • Sources indicate that waymo is Google’s robotaxi subsidiary, which has been operating autonomously on public roads in some form since 2017.
  • Recent findings suggest that the vehicles can be hailed through Waymo’s app, and operate with no driver in the driver’s seat, 24/7 in the covered areas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waymo has pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after the California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the manufacturer to pause highway operation in the state, following a viral video showing a Waymo trying to pass a police blockade.

Sources indicate that waymo is Google’s robotaxi subsidiary, which has been operating autonomously on public roads in some form since 2017. It has now expanded to 15 areas, recently adding another 250 square miles just last month.

Recent findings suggest that the vehicles can be hailed through Waymo’s app, and operate with no driver in the driver’s seat, 24/7 in the covered areas. Since it can operate at any time but only within geofenced areas, this counts as “level 4” autonomy, as compared to the level 2 autonomy available on most consumer vehicles.

Until recently, Waymo only operated on city streets. These are more complex than highways, but lower speed. Accidents are more common on city streets than on highways, but can be more spectacular on highways given the higher speeds involved.

It has been revealed that most driver assist systems have been rolled out gradually, starting with highways, due to this lower complexity. But Waymo started with city streets first, bucking that trend.

The tech giant started offering rides on highways late last year, but only in limited markets. It had been testing highway operation for several years prior, typically with a driver and with no public ridership.

Industry observers note that everything was going pretty well, with Waymo declaring its autonomous vehicles have stopped 841 injuries over the course of their 271 million miles of operation. And in terms of competition, Waymo is far ahead of Tesla’s Robotaxi effort.

But then, the viral internet stepped in. Last week, a video surfaced showing a Waymo trying to pass two police cars who were trying to slow down traffic on I-280 in Northern California. This is one of the main routes through Silicon Valley, and the opening of highway operations drastically reduced ride times in the area.

In a recent development, the video shows two police cars behind a construction vehicle, lights on and spread out across the freeway. Then it pans to show a Waymo vehicle moving rapidly in the far left lane. One of the officers accelerates and swerves in front of the Waymo vehicle, at which point the Waymo swerves and slows down. (One media citation says that the video seems to have been sped up by the original poster, but we’ve embedded the short local news report on it above).

In response to this, the California DMV contacted Waymo and ordered the tech giant to pause highway operations while it examines the incident. The order was made on November 11, but wasn’t reported until today.

The DMV cited multiple instances of Waymo vehicles incurring into construction zones, not simply the one viral clip above. It noted that previous incidents had occurred and been noted, and corrective actions were implemented, but that the incidents keep happening.

Recent findings suggest that this is a very rare situation which Waymo handled poorly. Waymo will add this case to their their test suite. They'll probably ask the CHP for their in car videos of other cases and convert those to be additional test cases. Waymo has been very willing to admit when their vehicles make mistakes in rare situations and fix it so that it doesn't happen again.

Recent findings suggest that waymo's vehicles are compared against perfect driving and Waymo accepts that as an aspirational goal. I note Tesla lacks the confidence in their system to even apply for the California permit to begin autonomous testing.

DMV’s pause will remain until Waymo can demonstrate “effective corrective actions” have been taken.

Sources indicate that while the DMV’s order only applies to California highways, Waymo also paused highway operations in other states. It remains operating on city streets in all coverage areas.

Update: Waymo emailed us this statement after it saw this article.

“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do. Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”.

  • After introducing the Neira Concept at the 2026 Gaikindo Indonesia International Auto Show (GIIAS) in July, Hyundai is gearing up to open pre-orders on November 20.
  • The Neira is a pretty “massive” deal as Hyundai’s first locally produced seven-seat electric SUV in Indonesia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai revealed the production-ready Neira EV for the first time, a three-row, seven-seat electric SUV set to launch in Indonesia on November 20.

After introducing the Neira Concept at the 2026 Gaikindo Indonesia International Auto Show (GIIAS) in July, Hyundai is gearing up to open pre-orders on November 20.

The Neira is a pretty “massive” deal as Hyundai’s first locally produced seven-seat electric SUV in Indonesia.

Ahead of its official debut on Friday at GAIKINDO Auto Week (GAW) 2026, Hyundai offered a closer look at the upcoming Neira.

Industry observers note that the electric SUV is essentially a Hyundai-badged version of the Kia Carens Clavis EV that debuted last year. Aside from the Hyundai logos, a few minor tweaks to the front and rear ends, and newly introduced wheels and headlights, it’s a near replica.

Inside, both are equipped with dual 12.3″ instrument display and center navigation screens, plus an added climate control panel.

Hyundai didn’t reveal battery or powertrain specs, but the Neira is expected to use the same 42 kWh and 51.4 kWh battery packs as the Carens Clavis EV. The former offers an MIDC range of up to 251 mi (404 km), while the latter has up to 304 mi (490 km) on a single charge.

Both batteries can be charged from 10% to 80% in around 39 minutes using a 100 kW DC fast charger.

The Kia Carens Clavis is 4,550 mm long, 1,800 mm wide, and 1,708 mm tall, with a 2,780 mm wheelbase, so Hyundai’s Neira will likely be about the same size, if not slightly bigger.

Hyundai noted the Neira has four key advantages: A higher ground clearance, Hyundai Bluelink connectivity tech, a Blind-spot View Monitor (BVM), and easy third-row access.

A post shared by Hyundai Motors Indonesia (@hyundaimotorindonesia).

Ahead of its upcoming launch, Hyundai is taking the electric 7-seater on a trip to prove its capabilities, going from Kilometer Nol in Banda Aceh to Banda Neira, which is about 4,000 kilometers (about 2,500 miles).

While Hyundai may export the Neira EV to overseas markets like India, don’t expect it to reach the US.

Hyundai already sells a three-row, seven-seat electric SUV, the IONIQ 9, which is built at Hyundai’s Metaplant in Georgia.

#122412. Iceland’s first wind farm comes with a water-saving bonus

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1319 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Iceland’s first wind farm comes with a water-saving bonus

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.
  • It has been revealed that vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads.
  • In a recent development, landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power company, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.

It has been revealed that vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads. And Iceland’s windiest months coincide with the time of year when less water flows into its reservoirs.

In a recent development, landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power company, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026. The first 14 turbines are online; another 14 will be installed in a second phase, and the entire wind farm is expected to be operating by the end of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that once complete, Vaðölduver will have 120 megawatts (MW) of capacity. When I met with the folks at Landsvirkjun in Reykjavik last month, they told me that’s enough to power the equivalent of 90,000 Icelandic households. Vaðalda’s electricity feeds into the grid and is sold through power purchase agreements.

In a recent development, vaðölduver sits on a lava-and-sand plain east of the Þjórsá River, south of Sultartangi Dam. Landsvirkjun already operates seven hydropower stations in the surrounding Þjórsá and Tungnaá region.

The wind farm was sited in this region of Iceland because the seasons line up nicely.

The winds are strongest in winter, when inflows into hydropower reservoirs can be low. In summer, wind speeds tend to drop, but glacial melt increases water availability for the hydropower system.

In a recent development, when the wind turbines are generating plenty of electricity, Landsvirkjun can ease off hydropower and leave more water in its reservoirs. When the wind drops, hydropower can pick up more of the demand.

That gives the utility more control over when it uses its stored water and helps that water go further.

German wind turbine maker Enercon manufactured Vaðölduver’s turbines. The project also includes a service and maintenance agreement with Enercon.

Sources indicate that landsvirkjun had a decade of experience operating pilot wind turbines before building Vaðölduver. One substantial thing they learned: They didn’t need tall towers to find plenty of wind.

It has been revealed that there’s little vegetation or other surface obstructions across this unique, exposed landscape. That allows the turbines to capture productive winds closer to the ground than they could at a more wooded or sheltered location.

According to recent reports, “Lower” is relative, of course. The turbines still reach 150 meters (492 feet) at their highest blade tip.

The wind farm covers 17.1 square kilometers (6.6 square miles). Twenty-five turbines are rated at 4.26 MW each, and the remaining three at 4.5 MW. Landsvirkjun’s presentation puts annual generation at 440 GWh and lists a P50 net efficiency figure of 43%, which is considered strong for onshore wind.

The ability to tap into existing infrastructure was a major factor in Landsvirkjun’s site selection. Where a wind farm goes affects its cost, its environmental footprint, and the people who live nearby.

Landsvirkjun also identifies active engagement with communities and other stakeholders as essential to building wind projects. At Vaðölduver, the immediate task is to finish the remaining 14 turbines while the first phase completes its trial runs.

The tech giant sees wind as a potential third pillar of Iceland’s electricity supply alongside hydropower and geothermal. Vaðölduver demonstrates how those resources can work together, with wind adding generation while helping conserve stored water.

Recent findings suggest that iceland is a world leader in clean energy. It generates nearly 100% of its electricity from renewable sources, combining hydropower fueled by glacial runoff and rivers (around 70%) and geothermal energy (around 30%).

Over 90% of Icelandic households use direct geothermal hot water for space heating and hot water, while the remaining homes use renewable electricity.

Industry observers note that but it’s got the same grid capacity challenges as every other country. Adding wind – and anything else that uses power – means paying close attention to what the grid can handle. Iceland has an isolated transmission system, so maintaining stability and ensuring sufficient capacity are increasingly vital as the country develops more projects.

Recent findings suggest that while in Reykjavik, I met with the Minister of the Environment, Energy and Climate, Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson, who told me that the Icelandic grid’s capacity is expected to grow from 20 TWh to 24-25 TWh within a decade. Jóhannsson also said that he is pro-data center and that investors are keen to establish more of them in the country.

When I asked Jóhannsson and his team, as well as the teams at Landsvirkjun and publicly owned ON Power, Iceland’s second-largest electricity generator and largest EV charger network, about grid expansion plans to handle that pipeline, they all said that legislative reforms were being passed to speed up energy permitting processes. There is also financing in place to grow the grid. The physical transmission network is being expanded, but the process is slow because NIMBYism is creating bottlenecks.

In learning about newly introduced and completed Icelandic power projects during my visit, it was apparent that the companies in the power and geothermal heat sector regularly collaborate on projects – everyone brings their expertise to the table and works for the common good (yes, really).

In a recent development, but what was striking in discussions about grid expansion was that there seemed to be no plans to pitch in with the Icelandic transmission system operator (TSO), Landsnet hf. It seemed that the plan was to let the TSO come up with the solutions on its own. At most, Jóhannsson’s team said its legislative reform “opened the door” to possible grid innovations.

When I asked the Landsvirkjun team whether they were considering working with the TSO on distributed energy resource (DER) projects like virtual power plants and onsite battery storage for its heavy-industry clients, which make up 80% of its business, they stated they hadn’t considered it.

It has been revealed that I often wonder why Quebec hasn't followed this strategy. They have huge dams with world-leading power connections, and one of the issue they are facing is a lack of water to refill those dams, due to several years of relative drought. I know it costs a lot to build wind power up north, but siting a project there would re-use their massive investment in power lines. The dams would act as gigantic batteries, because they wouldn't need to drain their reservoirs when the wind is blowing.

In a recent development, iceland has earned its reputation as a clean energy leader. Bringing that same collaborative and creative approach to expanding its grid would help it keep setting an example for the rest of the world.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin fell to $57,470 on Wednesday as hotter-than-expected US core inflation and the announcement of new tariffs intensified selling across risk assets.
  • The Nasdaq 100 extended its losses to 2.9%, reversing the optimism that followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO earlier this week.
  • Recent findings suggest that data released by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin fell to $57,470 on Wednesday as hotter-than-expected US core inflation and the announcement of new tariffs intensified selling across risk assets.

The Nasdaq 100 extended its losses to 2.9%, reversing the optimism that followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO earlier this week.

Recent findings suggest that data released by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis on Nov. 25 indicated that the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.8% annually in October, its second-highest reading since April 2023.

Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, accelerated to a three-year high of 3.3%, beating economists' 3.2% forecast.

Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said the stronger-than-expected core reading indicated that price pressures were spreading across the economy beyond the recent energy shock.

According to recent reports, the report follows increases in both consumer and producer price inflation, with financial markets now assigning a greater than 97% probability to a quarter-point interest rate hike on Dec. 9.

That would mark the Fed's second rate increase of 2026, lifting its benchmark rate to between 4% and 4.25%. Twelve months ago, investors were anticipating three rate cuts this year.

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump's administration confirmed a new round of proposed tariffs targeting 14 major US trading partners following an eight-month investigation into foreign industrial policies.

The measures include additional tariffs of 20% on Chinese imports, up to 35% on Vietnamese goods, and up to 25% on imports from India, Taiwan and South Korea. The European Union faces duties of up to 20%.

The announcement opens another front of uncertainty for investors already grappling with the prospect of higher borrowing costs.

André Dragosch, Bitwise's European head of research, expects this market turbulence to persist, saying:.

“Market volatility will likely stay elevated in the short term until uncertainty around inflation and the outlook for monetary policy fully resolve.”.

The deteriorating macroeconomic backdrop comes as Bitcoin investors show signs of financial distress comparable to the depths of the 2022 bear market.

Blockchain analytics firm Glassnode reported that Bitcoin's correlation with the Nasdaq 100 has climbed to its highest level since September 2022. Over the past 60 trading days, Bitcoin has consistently underperformed the index on both up and down days.

That weakness has coincided with a surge in demand for downside protection across Bitcoin's options market.

According to Glassnode, the seven-day average put-to-call trading volume ratio reached 1.7 last week, its highest level since June 2022. The corresponding ratio for outstanding options contracts climbed to its highest level since May 2021.

“The last rush into puts like this was June 2022. Bitcoin was near $20,000 in the middle of the capitulation. The final low came five months later, below $17,000.”.

The growing pessimism extends beyond derivatives markets. CryptoQuant CEO Ki Young Ju stated Bitcoin investors are underwater at historical capitulation levels, while Glassnode reported that realized losses, relative to recent capital inflows, had reached their highest level since FTX collapsed in November 2022.

Institutional demand has also weakened, with US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds registering $4.9 billion in net outflows this month.

Glassnode identified Bitcoin's realized price of $53,200 as the next major threshold should the cryptocurrency close decisively below its June closing low of $58,500.

In a recent development, every previous major Bitcoin bear market saw prices fall below the realized price before bottoming out. Reaching that level would require a further 7.4% decline from Wednesday's reported low, as investors confront the prospect of tighter monetary policy and a prolonged withdrawal of institutional capital.

#122398. What Is Pons? The Robinhood Chain Meme Coin Launchpad Explained

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1564 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Decrypt ↗ Open Full Page

What Is Pons? The Robinhood Chain Meme Coin Launchpad Explained

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when Robinhood switched on its own Robinhood Chain blockchain on July 1, 2026, the trading app's stock tokens were supposed to be the main attraction.
  • Pons became the busiest place to make them.
  • Recent findings suggest that that openness can also be exploited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when Robinhood switched on its own Robinhood Chain blockchain on July 1, 2026, the trading app's stock tokens were supposed to be the main attraction. Instead, much of the early activity came from meme coins: tokens built around a joke or an internet trend.

Pons became the busiest place to make them. Like Pump.fun on Solana, it lets anyone pick a name, ticker and image and have a tradable token minutes later, without writing code. Its fees briefly made it one of the highest-earning protocols in crypto, and its own token, PONS, went on to list on Kraken and Coinbase.

Recent findings suggest that that openness can also be exploited. In September 2026, an onchain analyst alleged that one group had used Pons rolls out to extract millions of dollars from buyers.

This guide explains what Pons is, how its two generations of contracts work, what the PONS token does, and the risks.

Pons is a token launch protocol running on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 network built on Ethereum using Arbitrum's technology, and its website and documentation are published by Pons Labs, LLC.

Every token launched through Pons is a standard ERC-20 token with a fixed supply, 1 billion tokens on V1 releases, that can never be increased. The creator gets no allocation set aside before trading opens.

Pons is also non-custodial. Its documentation states every launch and trade is a transaction the user's own wallet signs, and the platform never holds user funds.

It has been revealed that pons went live within days of Robinhood Chain's mainnet. It picked up most of the chain's launchpad activity after an early rival, Noxa, stopped accepting upcoming rolls out on July 11, 2026, according to Decrypt's reporting.

Pons has two generations of contracts, V1 and V2, and both remain live on Robinhood Chain.

In V1, a single transaction deploys the token and its trading pool, a Uniswap V3 pool paired with wrapped ETH (WETH), and locks the pool's liquidity so the creator can't withdraw it. Each launch costs 0.0005 ETH and carries a 1% trading fee, the documentation notes. A launch "graduates" once 4.2 ETH has been paired in its pool by default, but trading carries on in the same pool.

Sources indicate that V1 introduces are protected for their first two blocks: in the launch block, only the creator's initial buy can execute, and for the rest of the window no wallet can hold more than 5% of supply or buy more than 5.5%. Fees are split 70% to the creator and 30% to the protocol for current launches.

Recent findings suggest that V2 adds a bonding curve: a contract that holds a token's whole supply and sets its price by formula, rising as people buy and falling as they sell. According to the V2 documentation, the curve sells out, then "graduates" automatically into a Uniswap V4 pool, seeded with a fixed share of supply held back from the start. The pool's liquidity is then locked permanently; no unlock function exists.

V2 rolls out can be priced in ETH or in other assets Pons has approved, including tokenized stocks, in which case the creator is paid in that asset. Each trade pays a standard fee shared between Pons, the creator and an optional buyback, plus an optional creator tax that is capped by the protocol and fixed at launch.

Industry observers note that when a creator turns buybacks on, part of their own fee is spent buying their token back. Those tokens are locked in a vault and released over five years, split between the creator and the protocol.

PONS itself was launched through Pons's own legacy V1 factory, and its documentation uses PONS as the reference token for developers testing their integrations.

According to recent reports, "Sniping" means buying a large share of a upcoming token in its first seconds, often with bots, then selling into later buyers. Every V2 launch opens with a "snipe tax" of 99% on buys that decays to zero over five seconds, the documentation says.

The launching wallet and the creator's fee wallet are exempt automatically, and creators can name up to 32 more exempt addresses at launch "for a team bundling its opening buys across several wallets.".

That exemption became central to allegations published on September 27, 2026. Pseudonymous onchain analyst Wazz tweeted that a single operation had extracted at least $18.43 million from 53 Robinhood Chain launches between July 10 and September 21, 2026, mostly through Pons V2. Wazz said nearly every launch was sniped for 70% or more of its supply by bundles of 70 to 200 wallets.

I just uncovered the biggest serial Rugpulling and Extraction operation on Robinhood.

The same operation is linked 53 debuts within a 2 month period.

Total Extracted: $18.43 MILLION.

very likely more this is just what I could directly link.

🧵 https://t.co/wS62KAbvv5 pic.twitter.com/BSxZL9wU44.

— Wazz (@WazzCrypto) September 27, 2026.

The Block reviewed the onchain data and found that creators of nine Pons V2 debuts had exempted 15 to 25 wallets each from the snipe tax, which then bought out the bonding curve in a single transaction. The creator and those wallets held 82% to 86% of supply after the opening buys. The Block did not independently replicate Wazz's $18.43 million total.

Sources indicate that on September 3, 2026, Pons generated $5.95 million in daily fees, briefly out-earning Robinhood Chain itself and ranking fourth among all protocols tracked by DefiLlama, Decrypt reported. Pons fees drove Robinhood Chain to a record of about $6 million in daily fees in early September 2026, The Block reported.

According to recent reports, on September 5, 2026, blockchain analytics firm Arkham tweeted that crypto market maker Wintermute appeared to be buying PONS slowly in a series of small purchases, and held just over $3 million of the token. Wallets that Arkham attributes to Wintermute held about 3.4 million PONS at the time, and about 7.4 million as of November 2026.

As of November 20, 2026, DefiLlama put Pons's cumulative fees at about $205 million. Of that, $137 million came in September 2026 alone; fees fell to about $17 million in October 2026.

Sources indicate that PONS is the ERC-20 token tied to the Pons launchpad, with a fixed supply of 1 billion. Its link to the platform is a buyback.

According to recent reports, according to the V1 documentation, 80% of the protocol's fees are used to buy PONS on the market through an automated process and send it to a burn address, permanently removing it from circulation. The remaining 20% pays for infrastructure and the Pons team. Kraken's listing notice describes the same mechanism.

As of November 20, 2026, CoinGecko data indicates about 669 million PONS in circulation, out of a fixed supply of 1 billion.

You can track PONS's latest price on Decrypt's price page.

Industry observers note that PONS trades in Uniswap pools on Robinhood Chain. Binance Wallet added it to its Binance Alpha tier on September 2, 2026, and Kraken opened PONS trading on September 25, 2026, with access through the Kraken App and Instant Buy to follow once liquidity allows. Coinbase Markets tweeted on October 6, 2026, that it had added PONS to its listing roadmap, and noted the next day that its PONS-USD pair would open later that day, if liquidity conditions were met.

Pons has flagged several changes still to come. Its V1 documentation indicates the 80% share of protocol fees used to buy back PONS is not yet fixed in its contracts, but will become "immutable, decentralized, and automated" in a future release.

It has been revealed that on V2, three security firms (SB Security, Dingbats and Pashov Audit Group) are reviewing the contracts, and Pons says it will publish their reports in full, including any findings it did not accept, once the reviews close. Until then, its documentation tells consumers to treat V2 as unaudited, and only whitelisted addresses can create V2 tokens.

Industry observers note that pons also faces competition on its home chain. Uniswap, already Robinhood Chain's main exchange, debuted its own launchpad, Pools.trade, on August 5, 2026. It charges no launchpad fee, locks each launch's liquidity permanently, and offers a "crowd launch" option designed to resist bundling. Within its first days, Pools.trade took about half of Robinhood Chain's launchpad volume, Decrypt's Morning Minute newsletter reported. The newsletter noted that Uniswap can afford to forgo launchpad fees because it earns from its other products, which most dedicated launchpads cannot.

It has been revealed that pons has since kept the larger share of fees. As of November 2026, DefiLlama revealed Pons collecting about $5.6 million in fees over the previous 30 days, against about $115,000 for Pools.trade. The two charge different rates, though: Pools.trade's trading fee is 0.25%, while Pons's standard fee is 1%.

V2's tokenized-stock pairs link Pons introduces to the stock tokens Robinhood built the chain to carry, which ties Pons's prospects to Robinhood Chain itself. On Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call on October 27, 2026, CEO Vlad Tenev said the growth of the chain and its ecosystem had exceeded the manufacturer's expectations, and that Robinhood was investing in how to support the chain's developer community.

#122392. Tech Report: The Kids Are Outside: The Rise of the Adult Children’s ADU

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (978 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Kids Are Outside: The Rise of the Adult Children’s ADU

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home.
  • While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.
  • Sources indicate that blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home. And while Sam is thriving professionally as a sales rep with his own place, they never expected that his house would be in their backyard. But the nightmarish Bay Area real estate market made a 400-square-foot ADU (accessory dwelling unit) on his parents’ property, complete with a separate entrance and direct street access, seem like the best option for the 32-year-old. “It was becoming difficult for him to afford rent while also saving toward eventually buying a place of his own,” Diane tells AD. “He’s close by, but it really feels like he has his own home.”.

While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.

Diane and Steve Weaver on their property’s ADU.

Sources indicate that blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis. These days a homebuyer needs an annual income between $110,000 and $113,000—well above the national average income of $64,220 per year—to comfortably afford a median-priced home in the US, which is currently priced at $434,900. While this has led some grown kids to move back into their childhood bedrooms, in cases where acreage allows, families like the Weavers are opting to be neighbors instead of housemates by setting up self-contained living spaces on the same lot as their single-family homes. In California, they’re certainly no outlier. The state has passed legislation specifically encouraging the construction of ADUs to address the housing shortage—which resulted in quadruple the number of ADU permits issued in the Golden State from 2017 to 2022.

Those in the ADU construction game say families like the Weavers make up an increasingly large slice of their business. Jeremy Nova, co-founder of the Colorado-based prefab ADU builder Studio Home, says ADUs for adult children are popular among his clients because the arrangement is mutually beneficial. The kids are afforded some independence and the ability to save money, “while for the parents, it can also be a long-term investment. The same space that houses an adult child today could eventually become a rental or a separate living space for a caregiver.” ADU builders on the opposite coast are seeing the same demand. Justin Olewack, president of Bolt Builders, says that ADUs for adult children are becoming a top request among his clientele in the DC, Virginia, and Maryland areas, where housing costs have risen 61 percent since 2016.

If it cuts costs and results in a sellable amenity down the line, perhaps moving back home isn’t the failure-to-launch scenario it was once seen as.

An ADU by Studio Home, built in the backyard of a Scottsdale, Arizona, family’s property.

Once a family’s adult child moves out of the property’s ADU, especially if it has a kitchen and bathroom, the structure can serve as a rental, providing passive income for retired parents. Tracy Noh, who hired John Brennan of BZBuild Co to build her daughter Eliza Bowen an ADU in Burbank, was thinking long-term with her compound planning. “An in-home apartment would require sharing the space of our 1,000-square-foot main home. And, as someone who works from home, the ADU seemed a better solution,” she says.

Noh and Eliza show off their Burbank ADU.

The living arrangement has also enabled Noh and her daughter to develop their own life paths. The structure gives her daughter a space in which she can become a young adult, and Noh the opportunity to step back from making the day-to-day household decisions. The former is learning how to manage her own household: planning meals, budgeting expenses, and making time for household chores.

“That change in dynamic also allows us both to remain much calmer in our interactions with each other,” Noh says. It’s not just because there’s a separate place for each of them to retreat to; Noh says she has “gained an enormous amount of respect for Eliza and her ability to manage her own home. It’s a fabulous opportunity to begin to build that adult-to-adult relationship with your child.”.

The interior of Tracy Noh’s ADU by BZBuild Co.

While modest ADUs serve single occupants just fine, more sizable ADUs allow a family’s adult children to bring their own kids in tow. Oren Amir, co-founder of SoCal builder GO Home Builders, points out that in his experience, the catalyst for aging parents to build an ADU for their adult children is almost never just the adult child themselves: It’s the grandchild they will be bringing with them. “The call comes a few months before or after a baby arrives,” he says. The grandparents don’t want to travel to visit their grandkids; they want them living nearby. Rent in Los Angeles is what stops people from saving, and early parenthood is when saving matters most, Amir says. An ADU in a grandparent’s backyard, therefore, lets the adult children stay in the neighborhood, raise the baby near help, and set some money aside for when the time comes to leave the nest for good. “Everyone gets what they need and nobody has to move in,” Amir says of the arrangement.

According to recent reports, while the Weaver family ADU is Sam’s for now, it could grow up to be a granny flat someday. “It’s possible that Sam might live in the main house and we could move into the ADU as we age,” claims Diane. “It gives us a lot of options for how the space can be used as our family’s needs change.”.

#122389. France’s Senate Rejects Rule Forcing Bitcoin Holders to Declare Self-Custody Wallets

📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bitcoinmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

France’s Senate Rejects Rule Forcing Bitcoin Holders to Declare Self-Custody Wallets

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • France’s Senate has rejected a proposal that would have forced bitcoin holders to report self-custody wallets worth €100,000 or more to the tax authorities, along with two other crypto tax measures in the 2027 budget.
  • According to recent reports, senators voted down two identical amendments on Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that the first, amendment I-2447, came from Sens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

France’s Senate has rejected a proposal that would have forced bitcoin holders to report self-custody wallets worth €100,000 or more to the tax authorities, along with two other crypto tax measures in the 2027 budget.

According to recent reports, senators voted down two identical amendments on Nov. 24 during debate on the first part of the 2027 finance bill. Both would have required taxpayers to declare crypto wallets they hold directly, outside a crypto service provider, when the total value inside reached at least €100,000 on Dec. 31 of the tax year.

Recent findings suggest that the first, amendment I-2447, came from Sens. Pascal Savoldelli and Pierre Barros and the Communist-led CRCE-K group. The second, amendment I-2992, came from Sen. Anne-Sophie Romagny and seven other senators. The government opposed both, and both were rejected.

Backers argued that France already makes taxpayers declare accounts on foreign crypto platforms, just like foreign bank accounts. Wallets that holders manage themselves, without an intermediary, escape any such obligation.

“They have become the digital equivalent of the undeclared safe,” the CRCE-K group wrote in its amendment, adding that tax authorities can’t see them, check gains on them or reach them in an estate or when a holder moves abroad.

Romagny’s version pointed to a gap in the numbers. Crypto holders in France realized €3.5 billion in gains in 2021, but only €400 million in digital assets were declared to the tax administration that same year, the amendment mentioned. It proposed fines of up to €10,000 for failing to declare.

The National Assembly had approved the same wallet rule on Nov. 3. It fell away the next day, when deputies rejected the entire revenue section of the budget. Senators then took up the same measure as an amendment to the budget.

Senators also rejected two other proposals from the CRCE-K group. Amendment I-2421 would have ended France’s tax deferral on swaps into electronic money tokens under the EU’s MiCA rules. That would have made converting bitcoin into a regulated stablecoin a taxable event.

Amendment I-2428 would have pulled crypto into France’s exit tax on unrealized gains for people who move their tax home abroad. It counted all crypto toward the €800,000 threshold, including coins held in self-custody or outside France.

It has been revealed that david Amiel, France’s minister for public action and accounts, argued against the wallet rule, saying the EU’s DAC8 directive already puts reporting duties on crypto firms. He said he was “more circumspect” about a “purely declarative” obligation that would not help authorities track crypto used in money laundering or tax fraud.

Recent findings suggest that the Senate’s finance committee also opposed the measures, and rapporteur general Christine Lavarde recommended rejecting all three. Lavarde noted that the wallet amendments drew on a recommendation from a Senate information report filed in June, and she left the question of the threshold to the government.

Self-custody has become a sore spot in France. DAC8 reporting on crypto platforms began on Jan. 1, 2026, and Bull Bitcoin has filed a legal challenge to annul France’s DAC8 rules over privacy concerns.

In a recent development, holders have also raised safety concerns. In August, bitcoiners were warned of wrench attacks after France’s tax authority confirmed a data breach affecting hundreds of thousands of people.

Industry observers note that reporting rules for platforms are still expanding. The National Assembly is set to debate approval of the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, or CARF, which shares crypto tax data between countries, on Dec. 7.

Sources indicate that the wallet fight is not fully over. The Senate is still working through the 2027 budget and is set to vote on the full bill on Dec. 9, before a joint committee of both chambers takes it up.

It has been revealed that the Tennessee plant adds a US refining step. Korea Zinc is developing the facility, called Project Crucible, with US government backing. #122381. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: Inside the Psychedelic 1970s-Inspired Dystopian Sets

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1790 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: Inside the Psychedelic 1970s-Inspired Dystopian Sets

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins.
  • Industry observers note that lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena.
  • District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins. Before bringing a fresh installment of her bestselling dystopian saga to the major screen, the two join forces to envision how the fictional world of Panem will take shape. “I go to New York each time, and we sit in a conference room at Scholastic,” claims Lawrence, who has directed five of the franchise’s six films. “We go through the book page by page and beat out what we think the movie is going to look like.”.

Industry observers note that lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena. Set twenty-four years before the original The Hunger Games (2012) plotline, the prequel follows District 12’s sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada)—the future mentor (played by Woody Harrelson) to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson)—as he is selected to fight in the Second Quarter Quell, a particularly sadistic rendition of the Games held every twenty-five years.

District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.

Recent findings suggest that though the dystopia is set in a future North America, the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), drew from the architecture of 1940s and ’50s postwar Berlin to depict evil President Snow’s rise to tyranny. Set forty years later, Sunrise explores Panem at a new stage of its evolution. Designed by returning production designer Uli Hanisch, the film follows Haymitch from his impoverished mining district, which barely evolves throughout the series’s sixty-five year timeline, to the opulent Capitol, whose extravagance is expressed through a 1970s-inflected visual lexicon.

Recent findings suggest that “I realized the ’70s fall right smack in the middle between that movie and the originals, so we could lean into that,” states Lawrence. Hanisch and his team incorporated references to Andy Warhol, Studio 54, and the decade’s psychedelic color palette, appropriating its progressive spirit to convey the Capitol’s opulence and authoritarianism—and, particularly in the arena, using the aesthetic as a means of deception. “To turn the ’70s style from something progressive, liberal, young, and open-minded into something evil is a twist,” says Hanisch. “But that is the key to the entire film’s design.”.

In a recent development, haymitch and Maysilee as allies in the arena. The forest portion was filmed separately near Cologne, Germany.

Recent findings suggest that the stylistic choice is also a poignant nod to Collins’s original inspiration for the book series. The 1970s marked a transformation in American television: as color TVs became ubiquitous in households across the country, sporting spectacles, variety indicates, and beauty pageants flourished, establishing cultural touchstones that would help shape the contemporary reality programming Collins critiques and satirizes in The Hunger Games. “I was flipping through the channels one night between reality television programs and actual footage of the Iraq War, when the idea came to me,” Collins recalled in a 2018 interview with The New York Times. The juxtaposition inspired her to explore just-war theory for young people through an authoritarian dystopia in which mass entertainment is an instrument of political control.

From an abandoned rural steel mill to authoritarian monuments from postwar Berlin, the film draws on politically charged German sites to capture Panem at a pivotal stage in its political and architectural evolution.

Production Designer Uli Hanisch at the District 12 set. “District 12 is the most sentimental set to me because I’d known this site near my hometown my entire life,” Hanisch says.

Recent findings suggest that to recreate the Appalachian-inspired, deteriorating industrial landscape of District 12 that was shot in Atlanta in the original series, the production utilized a sprawling abandoned steel mill in Duisburg, Germany, Hanisch’s hometown. “I wish we had it in the original movies, because it is an unbelievable space,” Lawrence says of the post-industrial, rural landscape, which also appeared in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Hanisch’s first film in the franchise. “Everywhere you look is exactly how I have always imagined District 12.”.

Industry observers note that while District 12 was filmed near Atlanta in the original films, director Francis Lawrence’s fascination with German architecture brought production to Berlin for The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. It was there that he began collaborating with Berlin-based production designer Hanisch, who proposed this steel mill nearby his hometown for the new location. Upon seeing photographs, Lawrence exclaimed, “Are you kidding me? ... Let’s go tomorrow,” and promptly flew out to see it for himself.

The production designer added modest huts at the edge of a nearby quarry to recreate the Seam, home to Haymitch, his girlfriend Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), and fellow tribute Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), its humble dwellings contrasting the more prosperous merchant district inhabited by fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace).

“Unlike the Capitol, District 12 doesn't evolve stylistically throughout the films. Nobody is investing in it, and everything is gradually deteriorating,” Hanisch explains. The vivid purples and oranges of the Capitol’s ‘70s palette are notably absent, only appearing prominently in propaganda decorating the reaping square, including Hunger Games campaign materials and posters portraying Snow as Panem’s number-one Peacekeeper.

Druscilla in the Capitol before the tribute interviews, which is broadcast to all of Panem.

Recent findings suggest that in the Capitol, however, the architecture takes on a distinctly ‘70s flair. Rooted in the Roman concept of panem et circenses, or “bread and circuses,” from which Panem takes its name, the architecture reinforces the government’s manipulation through spectacle. In the background is Berlin's International Congress Centrum, a colossal, aluminum-clad convention center that opened in 1979, which Lawrence describes as “Cold War-era Berlin showing off in a modern way.” As West Berlin’s most expensive postwar building, the futuristic complex was publicly subsidised to showcase economic prosperity and technological advancement—an evocative backdrop for the Capitol’s own display of authoritarianism.

“It’s a time of peace for the Capitol with no rebel attacks, so Snow's had time to build the city up in a way that is an extravagant show of power,” Lawrence explains. The chariot parade, which introduces the tributes before the Games, similarly unfolds against the historically-charged Berlin Olympiastadion, which was designed by Werner March for the 1936 Olympics under Nazi Germany to project state power and an illusion of timeless permanence.

The upstairs library in Plutarch’s home, which he inherited from the Heavensbee dynasty. Reflecting the Capitol’s classic style, it contrasts the Plutarch’s modern downstairs salon which features Warhol-inspired portraits, including one of director Lawrence.

Sources indicate that the Capitol's grandeur is also exhibited inside the mansion of Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a cameraman with historic ties to Panem’s ruling class. “This was one of my favorite sets because of the scope and scale” Lawrence says, noting how its excess reflects the dynasty's immense wealth. Filmed at Berlin's late-1960s modernist Congress Center, the circular residence required twenty-five vans of retro-modern furniture to fill it. The salon, decked in vibrant 1970s furnishings and Warhol-inspired art, showcases Plutarch's modern sensibilities, in stark contrast to the upstairs library inherited from his family. “We wanted to distinguish Plutarch from the dynasty he comes from,” Lawrence explains, reflecting on how the expansive volumes must be a facade of intellectual sophistication.

It has been revealed that the set decoration department spent weeks hand-folding and assembling thousands of hollow cardboard books, interspersed with real volumes, including a collection of Edgar Allan Poe’s poetry, which Plutarch references to Haymitch. “We imagined Plutarch might actually be the first Heavensbee to read some of those books,” Hanisch says. “He even says the library is one of the few worthwhile things his ancestors accomplished.”.

The library's custom-built curved bookshelves envelope the characters, symbolising the insularity of Capitol society. “Circles represent both inclusion and exclusion,” Hanisch claims. “If you are in the circle, you're in. And if you're not, you're out.” As fans of the franchise will know, Plutarch (originally played by Philip Seymour Hoffman) later reveals himself as a double agent and leader of the underground rebellion against Snow’s regime.

The aspect ratio expands as Haymitch ascends into the eye-shaped arena, emphasizing the landscape’s immersive scale and beauty. While scouting locations, Lawrence drew inspiration from the dramatic landscapes in Terrence Malick’s A Hidden Life. “I had that in my head, only it was a little trippier. The Asturias were perfect,” he recalls. The kaleidoscopic design also inspired the official logo of the 50th Hunger Games, extending the arena’s psychedelic imagery into the Capitol’s propaganda.

The Quarter Quell arena, in particular, embodies the surreal, fantastical ethos of the 1970s that permeates the film, illustrating how the Capitol exploits beauty to disguise its underlying manipulation and brutality. “As I was reading with Suzanne, I stated there was an Alice in Wonderland-like element to it, which made me think of the song ‘White Rabbit,’ which made me think of the late ’60s, early ’70s,” Lawrence recalls. “That kind of broke something open for me.”.

Designed in the shape of an eye, the eight to ten mile arena serves as a metaphor for the Capitol's omnipresent surveillance. A golden Cornucopia forms its pupil; vibrant meadows its iris; and the surrounding mountain ranges its whites. In the book, Haymitch describes the especially lethal arena masquerading as an idyllic landscape as a “poisonous beauty of an arena.”.

Industry observers note that lawrence and Haymitch in the arena. The physical flowers were concentrated in the foreground, while visual effects extended the colorful landscape into the distance.

Seeking to capture as much natural landscape as possible, Hanisch and location manager Klaus große Darrelmann discovered a remote valley in Asturias, Spain, surrounded by the Cantabrian Mountains. Transforming the isolated valley into a psychedelic paradise proved an enormous undertaking.“The arena was our nemesis,” indicates Hanisch, recalling how the production had to bring extensive resources to the remote terrain. “You can't even imagine how far away it was or how hard it was to get to.” Crews spent weeks individually installing hundreds of thousands of artificial flowers throughout the meadows and forests.

Industry observers note that despite the arena’s dreamlike beauty, water sources, flowers, and vegetation conceal deadly poisons. “It’s the most colorful and playful dystopia you’ll ever see,” producer Nina Jacobson states. Perhaps more than anywhere else in Panem, the arena encapsulates how the Capitol weaponizes the electric zeitgeist of the ‘70s as an instrument of control. “To have something so overwhelmingly beautiful and seductive but poisonous and deadly is very cruel,” Hanisch says. “That contradiction captures the mentality of Panem at this point in its history.”.

Electric power tool brand Greenworks is expanding its battery-forward lineup in a huge way with the launch of OPTIMUS, an all-upcoming, go-anywhere electric side-by-side utility vehicle that packs over 100 equivalent hp and a 40 mph top speed.

It has been revealed that first shown at Equip Exposition 2026 in Kentucky last month, the newly redesigned Greenworks OPTIMUS UTV is the biggest, baddest, and newest addition to the company’s battery-backed commercial ecosystem. Greenworks claims the fresh SxS brings together the brand’s purpose-built equipment and power platforms and is designed to work across the demands of its professional property maintenance customers.

“OPTIMUS has always been about pushing battery power beyond what the industry expects, and the UTV is a natural extension of that vision,” claims Yin Chen, CEO of Greenworks. “We’re bringing professionals more ways to put battery power to work, from the equipment they use to maintain properties to the utility vehicles and charging systems that support their entire operation.”.

Greenworks’ OPTIMUS is built around the firm’s 400V high-voltage electrical platform and mates a pair of compact electric motors that combine for 110 equivalent (?) hp. Those motors draw power from a 19 kWh lithium-ion battery pack with enough efficiency to hit a 40 MPH top speed and cover up to 68 miles of range under typical operating conditions.

When it’s time to haul, OPTIMUS offers buyers a 2,500 lb. towing capacity and 1,300 lb. payload capacity along with 11 full inches of ground clearance and a beefy, 6,000 lb. electric winch. Independent suspension, oversized all-terrain tires, torque vectoring differentials, and multiple terrain modes round out the spec sheet and a picture of a machine that’s designed to handle some seriously demanding off-road applications.

Looks expensive but for a gov or tech giant leasing or buying a new utv probably price completive with less headache.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the bitcoin price fell to near $57,500 on Wednesday morning, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data, as Wall Street opened sharply lower on a deepening technology selloff, hotter-than-expected core inflation and a fresh round of U.S.
  • Industry observers note that bitcoin slipped to $60,000 on Tuesday morning and lost that level later in the day.
  • The world’s largest cryptocurrency is down about 24% in November and on course for its worst month since 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the bitcoin price fell to near $57,500 on Wednesday morning, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data, as Wall Street opened sharply lower on a deepening technology selloff, hotter-than-expected core inflation and a fresh round of U.S. tariff proposals. Bitcoin had traded near $58,400 before the 8:30 a.m. ET data release.

Industry observers note that bitcoin slipped to $60,000 on Tuesday morning and lost that level later in the day. It has now given back all of Monday’s spike above $64,000, which faded within hours after Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO. The bitcoin price remains above the weekend low near $55,100, its lowest level in more than two years.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency is down about 24% in November and on course for its worst month since 2022. It has also lost more than 30% since the start of the year, as record ETF outflows, rising rate-hike bets and a slide in AI stocks have kept buyers on the sidelines.

It has been revealed that the selling spread from Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi fell 6.16% overnight, to Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled about 4% in early trading, while the S&P 500 fell about 3% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost about 2%. Nvidia sank more than 8% to near $142, and Micron and AMD each fell more than 9% as doubts over the returns on AI spending resurfaced.

Tariffs added to the risk-off mood. The Trump administration proposed fresh Section 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan and India, over what it calls excess industrial capacity. China faces a 20% duty on top of the 25% imposed in 2018, CNBC reported. The new duties would take effect after a public comment period, in January at the earliest.

Inflation came in hotter than expected. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.3% in October and 3.8% from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy and is the Fed’s preferred gauge, climbed 3.3% from a year ago, above the 3.2% economists had expected and up from 3.1% in September.

Growth also ran hot. Real gross domestic product increased at a 4.3% annual rate in the third quarter, the Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its second estimate, up from the 3.4% pace first reported. Reuters called it the fastest growth in three years, driven by consumer spending and business investment in AI.

The reports solidified bets on another rate increase, with traders pricing in a 98% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting. The 10-year Treasury yield fell more than 6 basis points to 4.84% as investors bought bonds for protection, but that offered little support to the bitcoin price.

ETF selling continues. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $231.6 million on Tuesday, less than half of Monday’s $569.7 million, their sixth straight session of outflows. November withdrawals reached about $4.94 billion through Nov. 24, putting the funds on course for their worst month since launching in January 2024.

Crypto stocks fell with the broader market. Strategy (MSTR) dropped about 8% to near $71 in early trading, after closing down 8.12% at $77.55 on Tuesday. MSCI is set to remove the manufacturer from its indexes on Nov. 30, and Monness, Crespi, Hardt & Co. cut its price target to $59. The bitcoin price now sits well below Strategy’s average purchase price of $75,446.

It has been revealed that coinbase (COIN) fell about 6% to near $96, while Robinhood (HOOD) lost nearly 6% and Circle (CRCL) slid more than 7%. Miners took heavier hits. IREN dropped about 11% and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell nearly 10%, while Riot Platforms (RIOT), which sold thousands of bitcoin earlier this month, was down nearly 8%.

In a recent development, U.S. stock and bond markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and reopen Friday for a half-day session, making Wednesday the last full trading day of the week. Investors will next look to the November jobs report on Dec. 4, the last major data point before the Fed’s rate decision on Dec. 9.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $57,500.

Industry News: Elderly Florida man leads police on wild 16 mph e-bike chase. Thank goodness they caught him

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that residents of Fresh Smyrna Beach, Florida, can finally breathe a sigh of relief.
  • According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).
  • The deputy attempted to stop Mitchell, who allegedly responded with a middle finger and some choice words before continuing on his way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that residents of Fresh Smyrna Beach, Florida, can finally breathe a sigh of relief. A dangerous menace to society has been taken off the streets after police apprehended a 75-year-old man accused of leading deputies on a high-stakes electric bike chase at speeds reaching a blistering 16 mph (26 km/h).

According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).

The deputy attempted to stop Mitchell, who allegedly responded with a middle finger and some choice words before continuing on his way.

What followed was apparently the world’s slowest police chase.

In a recent development, mitchell reportedly continued riding along the beach, eventually exiting onto city streets, where he allegedly rode against traffic before making it back to his home. Deputies followed him, and when Mitchell attempted to retreat into his garage, he reportedly resisted arrest by grabbing onto a golf cart and refusing to let go.

It has been revealed that the ordeal ended with Mitchell in custody, facing four charges, including felony fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, resisting an officer without violence, speeding on the beach, and riding outside the designated beach driving area. His bond was set at $4,000.

And just like that, another dangerous electric bicycle criminal was brought to justice. This was clearly a success story like no other, and American streets are now safer.

Industry observers note that now, before anyone gets too worked up, let’s be clear: I’m not suggesting that e-bike riders should be allowed to ignore traffic laws, endanger pedestrians, or flee from police. Reports indicate that Mitchell was riding recklessly around beachgoers, including children, and that’s certainly something worth addressing. And once he allegedly decided to flee from deputies, he turned what could have been a minor infraction into a much more serious situation.

But can we also acknowledge how absurd this whole thing is?

We’ve reached a point where a 75-year-old man riding a bicycle at 16 mph can end up the subject of a police pursuit and felony charges, while we’ve largely accepted that multi-ton vehicles routinely kill and seriously injure people on our roads as an unavoidable cost of modern transportation.

Sources indicate that every day, drivers speed through neighborhoods, roll through stop signs, stare at their phones, and operate vehicles capable of killing pedestrians with a moment’s inattention. Or perhaps I shouldn’t say ‘capable’, but rather that they do. 40,000 people every year die in the US from car violence. Yet somehow, electric bicycles have become one of the great transportation menaces of our time, despite contributing much, much less to major bodily harm or death.

And yes, there are absolutely legitimate concerns about dangerous riding. I’ve repeatedly argued that we need better enforcement, especially when it comes to teenagers riding high-powered electric dirt bikes and e-motos at 40 mph (64 km/h) down sidewalks and bike paths. Those aren’t electric bicycles, and treating them as such has created a real problem for everyone.

But if we’re going to devote police resources to cracking down on dangerous two-wheeled behavior, perhaps we could start there instead of turning a 1 mph beach ride into the crime of the century.

Sources indicate that what is absurd is that he didn't simply stop and follow the officer's directions to slow down. If he is going to try to flee from the police by riding dangerously including going against traffic then he should face charges. As presumably a first time offender, he'll be given probation if he agrees not to do it again.

Sources indicate that to be fair, Mitchell’s alleged behavior after being stopped certainly didn’t help his case. But the larger point remains: our priorities around road safety have become wildly distorted.

We’ve normalized the dangers of cars so thoroughly that we barely blink at the daily carnage they cause, yet we’re increasingly treating comparatively low-speed electric bicycles as an existential threat to public safety.

I’m all for enforcing sensible e-bike rules. I’m all for throwing the book at major infractions and scofflaws who pose a public menace. But I’m also for applying a little perspective.

Because if a 75-year-old man riding an electric bicycle at 16 mph is among our most pressing transportation safety concerns, then I have some very good news about the state of our roads. But unfortunately, there is no good news to share today.
